# You're the Dev *and* the Security Champ. That's Not a Pep Talk.

Someone put "security champion" next to your name. You still ship features. You still own bugs. Now you're also the person who gets the scanner noise, the threat model invite, and the "can you just look at this CVE?" ping.

That role is real. The unpaid-second-job version of it is also real. Official AppSec frameworks say so out loud. Read them before you pretend the title alone fixes anything.

## What a security champion actually is

OWASP's Developer Guide defines a Security Champion as a member of a software development team who is the liaison between Information Security and developers. Goal: embed security into how the team builds, not leave it as a ticket that lands after merge ([OWASP Developer Guide overview](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/08-culture-process/02-security-champions/)).

The champion can be a developer, tester, product manager, or another role on the team. Enthusiasm and willingness to learn matter more than a CISSP. Typical work called out in that same overview: researching, verifying, and prioritizing security and compliance defects; joining risk/threat assessments and architectural reviews; helping shrink the attack surface; sitting in periodic briefings so the team actually builds expertise instead of vibes.

OWASP SAMM (Software Assurance Maturity Model) puts the same idea under Governance → Education and Guidance → Organization and Culture. Maturity level 1 for that stream is blunt: identify a Security Champion within each development team ([SAMM EG stream B](https://owaspsamm.org/model/governance/education-and-guidance/stream-b/)).

SAMM's activity text is even more specific about the job you just inherited:

- Set hours per week for Information Security related work (not "whenever you have free time")
- Extra training so you can act as a software security subject-matter expert
- Help research, verify, and prioritize security and compliance defects
- Show up for risk assessments, threat assessments, and architectural reviews
- Brief the project team on security issues so the whole squad sees the backlog, not just you
- Review external testing results before they dump into the application backlog

That is a job description. It is not "forward every Alert email and hope."

## The tension nobody puts on the LinkedIn post

You still have sprint commitments. Security work does not magically subtract story points.

OWASP is explicit that champions are often taking on an **extra** role on top of the one they already have, and that the program has to support their well-being or you get disillusionment and burn-out ([OWASP Security Champions Guide summary](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/08-culture-process/02-security-champions/02-security-champions-guide/)). The Developer Guide overview says the same thing: if possible, give the champion time for InfoSec work, and you may have to negotiate that with development management ([overview](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/08-culture-process/02-security-champions/)).

If your manager celebrates the title and then schedules zero capacity, that is not a mature program. That is a name tag.

The OWASP Security Champions Manifesto lists the guardrails that keep this from becoming martyrdom: secure management support, trust your champions, create a community, reward responsibility, invest in your champions, anticipate personnel changes ([manifesto](https://securitychampions.owasp.org/manifesto/)). "Invest" here means personal growth: training, conferences, recognition, not another Slack channel and a badge emoji.

SAMM's quality criteria for the champion role also assume training happened, that AppSec and Dev get periodic status from the champion, and that external test results get reviewed before they become backlog sludge ([SAMM stream B](https://owaspsamm.org/model/governance/education-and-guidance/stream-b/)). If none of those are true where you work, you are wearing the title without the program.

## What "good" looks like when you are still shipping code

Use the frameworks as a checklist against your real week:

1. **Named hours.** SAMM expects a set number of hours per week for InfoSec activity. Put them on the calendar. If leadership will not protect them, escalate with the SAMM/OWASP language, not with guilt.
2. **Liaison, not lone wolf.** You are the bridge to InfoSec, not a replacement AppSec team of one ([Developer Guide overview](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/08-culture-process/02-security-champions/)).
3. **Triage before heroics.** Research, verify, prioritize. Do not swallow every scanner finding as personal debt.
4. **Show the team the queue.** Periodic reviews so security is a team problem, not your private inbox ([SAMM](https://owaspsamm.org/model/governance/education-and-guidance/stream-b/)).
5. **Demand the program pieces.** Training, community, recognition, succession plan. The manifesto calls those principles, not nice-to-haves ([manifesto](https://securitychampions.owasp.org/manifesto/)).

OWASP's Security Champions Guide is deliberately not one-size-fits-all. Pick the pieces your org can actually run ([guide home](https://securitychampions.owasp.org/), [Developer Guide summary](https://devguide.owasp.org/en/08-culture-process/02-security-champions/02-security-champions-guide/)). A custom thin program beats a copied manifesto poster nobody funded.

If your title is champion and your calendar is still 100% feature work, you do not have a security champion program. You have a risk with a sticky note on it.

## **Chris's take:** The job is liaison: make sure the practices exist and the team is actually following them. What I keep seeing is the opposite — the team treats the champion as the person who just takes care of all things security. Measure the role by what leaves your inbox, not what enters it. If after a quarter you're still the only person who can close a finding, the program failed, even if leadership loves the title.
